all_historical_figures.name: Śūlinī, Dhūmāvatī, Kubjikā, Eka-jaṭā, Cāmuṇḍā, Vārāhī
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the focus of Śāktāgama's cultic rituals, in contrast to Devyāgama's focus on Devi as Brahman.

all_historical_figures.name: Lakṣmī-dhara
all_historical_figures.significance: His work, Saubhāgya-ratnākara, is cited for its explanation of Samayācāra as internal worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Vasiṣṭha, Sanaka, Śuka, Sanandana, Sanat-kumāra
all_historical_figures.significance: Ascribed as authors of the five 'śubhāgama-pañcaka' texts associated with Samayācāra.

all_historical_figures.name: Patañjali
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of the Yoga-sūtra, his concept of Kriyā-yoga is used to explain the 'combined' approach of Devyāgama.

all_historical_figures.name: Nāka-maudgalyāyana
all_historical_figures.significance: Quoted for the idea that Vedic study (svādhyāya) is itself a form of penance (tapas).

all_historical_figures.name: Raghunath Misra
all_historical_figures.significance: Editor of the cited edition of Pārānanda-tantra (Varanasi, 1985).

all_historical_figures.name: Aditi
all_historical_figures.significance: Presented as the most significant goddess in the Ṛgveda and a precursor to the concept of Devī as the primordial, infinite mother.

all_historical_figures.name: Dakṣa-Prajāpati
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a paradox where he is both the father and son of Aditi, illustrating common divine origins.

all_historical_figures.name: Yāska
all_historical_figures.significance: His work, Nirukta, is cited multiple times for its interpretations of Vedic terms and concepts, including Aditi and the nature of deities.

all_historical_figures.name: Skanda-svāmi
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited for his commentary on the Ṛgveda, interpreting the meaning of 'Aditi'.

all_historical_figures.name: Sāyaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited for his commentary on Vedic hymns, explaining the distinction between Aditi and Diti.

all_historical_figures.name: Kullūka-bhaṭṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: Commentator on Manu-saṁhitā, quoted for citing Hārīta's division of śruti into 'vaidikī' and 'tāntrikī'.

all_historical_figures.name: Hārīta
all_historical_figures.significance: Quoted by Kullūka-bhaṭṭa for the concept of two types of śruti (Vedic and Tantric).

all_historical_figures.name: Vāk Āmbhṛaṇī
all_historical_figures.significance: The female seer of the Devī-sūkta (Ṛgveda, 10, 125), who identifies herself with the supreme reality.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhāskara-rāya-makhin
all_historical_figures.significance: A major authority cited for his commentary on Lalitā-sahasra-nāma and Bhāvanopaniśad, arguing that tantras align with the brahma-kāṇḍa of the Vedas.

all_historical_figures.name: Umā haimavatī
all_historical_figures.significance: Appears in the Kena Upaniṣad to reveal the nature of Brahman to the gods; identified as the Upaniṣadic version of Devī.

all_historical_figures.name: Āśvalāyana
all_historical_figures.significance: Figure in the Sarasvatī-rahasyopaniśad who teaches the secret knowledge of Sarasvatī.

all_historical_figures.name: Lopāmudrā, Krodha-muni (Durvāsa), Candra, Nandi, Prabhākara, Ṣanmukha, Parama-śiva, Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.significance: Founders of different Śrī-vidyā traditions mentioned in Tripurā-tāpinyupaniśad.

all_historical_figures.name: Ānanda, Kardama, Ciklīta
all_historical_figures.significance: Sons of Lakṣmī who are said to have perceived the hymns of the Śrī-sūkta.

all_historical_figures.name: Ādi-nārāyaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: The divine teacher in Saubhāgya-lakṣmyupaniṣad who instructs the sages.

all_historical_figures.name: Prajāpati
all_historical_figures.significance: The divine teacher in Sītopaniśad who explains the nature of Sītā.

all_historical_figures.name: Janaka
all_historical_figures.significance: The earthly father of Sītā, who appeared from a ploughshare.

all_historical_figures.name: Tumburu, Nārada, Rākā, Siñivālī, Hlādinī, Māyā, Svāhā, Svadhā
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as attendants of Vīra-lakṣmī in Sītopaniśad.

all_historical_figures.name: Lopāmudrā
all_historical_figures.significance: Represents one of the twelve principal traditions of Śrī-vidyā. Also associated with the Hādi-division.

all_historical_figures.name: Durvāsa
all_historical_figures.role: First promulgator of a vidyā; Author of Devi-mahimnah-stava
all_historical_figures.significance: An important sage in the Śrī-vidyā tradition.

all_historical_figures.name: Manu
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the twelve founders of a vidyā.

all_historical_figures.name: Candra
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the twelve founders of a vidyā.

all_historical_figures.name: Madana (Kāmarāja)
all_historical_figures.significance: Originator of the Kāmarāja-vidyā, a primary form of Śrī-vidyā.

all_historical_figures.name: Kubera
all_historical_figures.significance: One of the twelve founders of a vidyā.

all_historical_figures.name: Agastya
all_historical_figures.significance: A prominent sage associated with a Śrī-vidyā lineage.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.role: First promulgator of a vidyā; Deity (Preserver)
all_historical_figures.significance: Listed as a founder and a primary deity in the Hindu pantheon.

all_historical_figures.name: Parama-śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Represents the ultimate source of a vidyā.

all_historical_figures.name: Benoytosh Bhattacarya
all_historical_figures.significance: Quoted for his definition of Samayācāra from his introduction to the Śakti-saṅgama-tantra.

all_historical_figures.name: Vasiṣṭha, Śuka, Śaunaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra
all_historical_figures.significance: Authors of the 'śubhāgama-pañcaka', the five auspicious scriptures associated with the Samaya approach.

all_historical_figures.name: Gauḍa-pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Subhagodaya', a text on Śrī-vidyā quoted multiple times.

all_historical_figures.name: Lakṣmīdhara
all_historical_figures.significance: Authoritative commentator on the 'Saundarya-laharī', whose interpretations are cited.

all_historical_figures.name: Vīra-rāghava
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of 'Śrī-vidyā-mantra-bhāṣya', quoted regarding the sixteenth kalā.

all_historical_figures.name: Sanatkumāra
all_historical_figures.significance: Source of the Sanatkumāra-samhitā, a text quoted for its views on the prohibition of external worship for advanced practitioners.

all_historical_figures.name: Gauḍapāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of the Subhagodaya-stava, which is cited for its formulation of the six kinds of identity contemplations in Samaya worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Muralidhar Jha
all_historical_figures.significance: Editor of the Puraścaryārṇava, a text quoted for its classifications of religious observances.
all_historical_figures.dates: The revised edition cited is from 1985.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhāskara-rāya-makhin
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as a prolific writer and the author of an excellent commentary on the Bhāvanopaniśat, a key text for Antaryāga.

all_historical_figures.name: Raghunāth Miśra
all_historical_figures.significance: Editor of the Pārānanda-tantra, a text cited for its enumeration of twenty cakras.

all_historical_figures.name: Durvāsa
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the author of the text Saubhāgya-cintāmaṇi, part of the 'miśra' tradition's literature.

all_historical_figures.name: Lakṣmīdhara
all_historical_figures.significance: His classification of the Kaula groups into five distinct sects (pūrva-kaulas, uttara-kaulas, etc.) is cited. His views on Vāmācārins and specific texts are also referenced.

all_historical_figures.name: Gauḍapāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Subhagodaya, a poetical work of fifty-two verses that formulates the Samaya outlook.

all_historical_figures.name: Śamkara
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the person to whom Saundarya-laharī is 'commonly but erroneously ascribed'.

all_historical_figures.name: Pārvati
all_historical_figures.significance: In the Mahā-nirvāṇa-tantra, she is the one who asks questions.

all_historical_figures.name: Śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: In the Mahā-nirvāṇa-tantra, he is the one who answers Pārvati's questions. He is also central to the philosophy discussed in Paraśurāma-kalpa-sūtra.

all_historical_figures.name: Mādhavānanda-nātha
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the author of Saubhāgya-kalā-druma.

complete_timeline.event: No specific historical events with dates are mentioned in this chapter. The content is theological and philosophical.

complete_timeline.significance: His commentary on Manu-saṁhitā is cited as evidence for the ancient division between Vedic and Tantric traditions.
The source text for the Devī-sūkta, Śrī-sūkta, and the concepts of goddesses like Aditi, which form the Vedic foundation of Devyāgama.
A major Tantric authority whose commentaries are used to argue for the alignment of Tantra (specifically Śrī-vidyā) with the gnostic (jñāna) part of the Vedas.
His Yoga-sūtra provided the framework for Kriyā-yoga, which is used in the text to conceptualize Devyāgama's synthetic approach.

complete_timeline.event: Composition of early Upaniṣads (like Kena Upaniṣad)
complete_timeline.significance: These texts established the philosophy of Brahman, with which Devyāgama aligns the concept of Devī.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the publication place of the cited edition of Pārānanda-tantra.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major historical center for Sanskrit scholarship and Hindu religious traditions.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the publication place of the author's own book, 'The Tantra of Sri-Cakra: Bhavanopaniśat'.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows the location of modern scholarship on the subject.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the northern corner of the central triangle in Śrī-cakra.
all_geographic_locations.significance: One of the primary Śakti Pīṭhas, a sacred center for goddess worship.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the southern corner of the central triangle in Śrī-cakra.
all_geographic_locations.significance: One of the primary Śakti Pīṭhas.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the third corner (svāgra-koṇastha) of the central triangle in Śrī-cakra.
all_geographic_locations.significance: One of the primary Śakti Pīṭhas, associated with Kāmākhyā.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the publication city of the revised edition (1985) of Puraścaryārṇava by Chowkhamba Sanskrit Pratishthana.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A modern center for the publication of Sanskrit texts.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the publication city of the Pārānanda-tantra (1985) by Sampūrṇanda Sanskrit University.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A historic and ongoing major center for Sanskrit learning and religious studies in India.

all_geographic_locations.context: The first of four regions in the Sammohana-tantra's classification. The tradition belongs to the Kahādi-division.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major center for a specific strand of Devi worship.

all_geographic_locations.context: The starting point of the Kerala region (from Anga to Mālava).
all_geographic_locations.significance: Defines the eastern boundary of the 'Kerala' region in this context.

all_geographic_locations.context: The end point of the Kerala region (from Anga to Mālava).
all_geographic_locations.significance: Defines the western boundary of the 'Kerala' region in this context.

all_geographic_locations.context: The second of four regions in the Sammohana-tantra's classification. The tradition is Hādi.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major center for the Hādi tradition and Tripura-sundarī worship.

all_geographic_locations.context: The starting point of the Kaśmira region (from Madra to Nepāla).
all_geographic_locations.significance: Defines the western boundary of the 'Kaśmira' region.

all_geographic_locations.context: The end point of the Kaśmira region and the starting point of the Ratha-krānta division.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Marks a boundary for two different classification systems.

all_geographic_locations.context: The third of four regions in the Sammohana-tantra's classification. The tradition is Kādi.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major center for the Kādi tradition and Kālī worship.

all_geographic_locations.context: The starting point of the Gauḍa region (from Assam to Sindhu).
all_geographic_locations.significance: Defines the eastern boundary of the 'Gauḍa' region.

all_geographic_locations.context: The end point of the Gauḍa region (from Assam to Sindhu).
all_geographic_locations.significance: Defines the western boundary of the 'Gauḍa' region.

all_geographic_locations.context: The fourth of four regions, described as 'all over the country'.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A pan-Indian classification for traditions not covered by the other three.

all_geographic_locations.context: Used as a geographical marker for the Krānta divisions (Viṣṇu-krānta, Aśva-krānta, Ratha-krānta).
all_geographic_locations.significance: A central dividing line in the territorial classification of tantras.

all_geographic_locations.context: The eastern boundary of the Viṣṇu-krānta division.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Defines the extent of the eastern tantric division.

all_geographic_locations.context: An alternative eastern boundary of the Viṣṇu-krānta division.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Suggests the influence or reach of these traditions far into Southeast Asia.

all_geographic_locations.context: The eastern boundary of the Aśva-krānta (western) division.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Likely refers to Greater China, indicating a far-reaching geographical scope for these traditions.

all_geographic_locations.context: The northern boundary of the Ratha-krānta division.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Indicates the northern extent of these tantric traditions.

complete_terminology_index.context: The main subject of the chapter, a school of thought and practice centered on the Goddess, distinct from Śāktāgama.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Āgama of the Śāktas (followers of Śakti)
complete_terminology_index.context: The broader tradition of Goddess worship from which Devyāgama is distinguished.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Āgama of the Śaivas (followers of Śiva)
complete_terminology_index.context: The tradition to which Śāktāgama is generally considered a division.
A specific group of eight Upaniṣads that form the scriptural basis of Devyāgama.
A topic covered in both Śāktāgama and Devyāgama.
A central doctrine and practice in both traditions, especially important in Devyāgama as its principal component.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Convention, doctrine, agreement; here signifies Vedic tradition
complete_terminology_index.context: The name of the path/ideology of Devyāgama.
The first of the 'seven conducts' and synonymous with Samayācāra.
The highest path in the tantric hierarchy, which disregards restrictions.
An anti-Vedic, antinomian path in the tantric hierarchy.
A path more aligned with Vedic norms than Vāmācāra.
The lowest of the three practitioner dispositions (bhāva), associated with Vedic-based paths.
The middling practitioner disposition, associated with Vāmācāra.
The highest practitioner disposition, associated with Kaulācāra.
The core practice of Devyāgama, involving mental and symbolic rituals.
Actual or external Vedic rituals, contrasted with antaryāga.
The combination of tapas, svādhyāya, and īśvara-praṇidhāna, presented as the method of Devyāgama.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Making become, mental contemplation, internal worship
complete_terminology_index.context: The central theme of Bhāvanopaniśad, meaning internal worship of Śakti.
The five articles used in some Śākta rituals: matsya (fish), māṁsa (flesh), madya (liquor), mudrā (stance), and maithuna (sexual union). Rejected by Devyāgama.
A key yantra in Śrī-vidyā, symbolically interpreted in Devyupaniṣads.

complete_terminology_index.term: वैष्णवादुत्तमं शैवं शैवाद्दक्षिणमुत्तमम्। दक्षिणादुत्तमं वामं वामात् सिद्धान्तमुत्तमम्। सिद्धान्तादुत्तमं कौलात्परतरं न हि ॥
complete_terminology_index.transliteration: vaiṣṇavāduttamaṁ śaivaṁ śaivāddakṣiṇamuttamam। dakṣiṇāduttamaṁ vāmaṁ vāmāt siddhāntamuttamam। siddhāntāduttamaṁ kaulātparataraṁ na hi ॥
complete_terminology_index.translation: Śaiva is superior to Vaiṣṇava, Dakṣiṇa is superior to Śaiva. Vāma is superior to Dakṣiṇa, Siddhānta is superior to Vāma. Kaula is superior to Siddhānta, there is nothing higher than Kaula.
complete_terminology_index.context: Quoted from Kulārṇava-tantra to illustrate the hierarchy of the 'seven conducts'.

complete_terminology_index.term: अन्तः शाक्ताः बहिः शैवाः सभायां वैष्णवा मता। नानावेशधराः कौला विचरन्ति महितले ॥
complete_terminology_index.transliteration: antaḥ śāktāḥ bahiḥ śaivāḥ sabhāyāṁ vaiṣṇavā matā। nānāveśadharāḥ kaulā vicaranti mahitale ॥
complete_terminology_index.translation: Within, they are Śāktas; outside, Śaivas; in assemblies, they are considered Vaiṣṇavas. Assuming various guises, the Kaulas wander the earth.
complete_terminology_index.context: Quoted from Śyāmā-rahasya to describe the secretive nature of Kaula practitioners.
The ultimate goal of Devyāgama and its principal practice, Śrīvidyā.
The collective name for the theory and practice of Devyāgama (goddess traditions).

complete_terminology_index.translation: Convention, rule, agreement; The ideology of internal worship.
complete_terminology_index.context: The name of the internal, Vedic-aligned school of Śrī-vidyā worship. The term itself is said to mean 'Vedic convention'.
A school of Tantra contrasted with Samaya, characterized by external worship and focus on lower chakras.
The central yantra (geometric diagram) used in Śrī-vidyā worship, representing the cosmos and the goddess.
The essential aspect and distinguishing feature of the Samaya approach.
The mode of worship attributed to the Kaulas and others, contrasted with antaryāga.
The serpent power, or latent spiritual energy, at the base of the spine, which is awakened and raised through the chakras in yogic practice.
The psychic energy centers in the subtle body, located along the spinal column.
The basal chakra, located at the perineum, associated with the earth element and worshipped by Kaulas.
The crown chakra, the highest psychic center, and the exclusive focus of worship for Samayins.
A major school of Śrī-vidyā, identified with the Samaya tradition.
A major school of Śrī-vidyā, contrasted with Kādi and associated with Lopāmudrā.
The core Samaya principle of the absolute identity of Śiva and Śakti, elaborated in five aspects.
Represents the unmanifest, transcendental point of unity (Śiva) from which creation emerges; the central point of the Śrī-cakra.
The famous fifteen-syllable mantra of Śrī-vidyā.
The transcendental, sixteenth aspect or syllable (Śrīm) added to the Pañcadaśī, representing the Mahā-nityā.
The central topic of the chapter, contrasted with external worship.
The conventional mode of worship with material objects, considered preliminary.
The sixteen or more services conducted with material objects in external worship.
Symbolic hand gestures used in external worship.

complete_terminology_index.term: बाह्यपूजा न कर्तव्या कर्तव्या बाह्यजातिभिः। सा क्षुद्रफलदा नृणां ऐहिकाथैकसाधनात् ॥
complete_terminology_index.transliteration: Bāhyapūjā na kartavyā kartavyā bāhyajātibhiḥ। Sā kṣudraphaladā nṛṇāṃ aihikārthaikasādhanāt ॥
complete_terminology_index.translation: External worship should not be done (by the advanced), it should be done by the outer classes. It gives petty results to men, as its only aim is worldly things.
complete_terminology_index.context: Quoted from Sanatkumāra-samhitā to prohibit external worship for advanced practitioners.

complete_terminology_index.term: अकृत्वा मानसं यागं न कुर्याद् बहिरर्चनम्
complete_terminology_index.transliteration: Akṛtvā mānasaṃ yāgaṃ na kuryād bahirarcanam
complete_terminology_index.translation: Without performing the mental sacrifice, one should not perform the external worship.
complete_terminology_index.context: A view suggesting internal worship must precede external worship.
A view that worship of god is a duty that cannot be given up.
The sin incurred by not performing a nitya-karma.

complete_terminology_index.term: कौलिकं कुर्वतः कर्म वैदिकं नाऽभिधीयते । विरोधादुभयं नष्टं तस्मादेकपथा चरेत्।।
complete_terminology_index.transliteration: Kaulikaṃ kurvataḥ karma vaidikaṃ nā'bhidhīyate । Virodhādubhayaṃ naṣṭaṃ tasmādekapathā caret।।
complete_terminology_index.translation: For one performing Kaulika rites, Vedic rites are not prescribed. Due to contradiction both are destroyed, therefore one should follow a single path.
complete_terminology_index.context: Quoted from Rudra-yāmala to show the antagonism between Kaulika and Vedic paths.
The subject of a three-fold classification from Meru-tantra.
The highest category of upāsanā.
The middle category of upāsanā.
The lowest category of upāsanā.
The four-fold conceptualization of identity that distinguishes antaryāga.
The central yantra in Śrī-Vidyā, used in both external and internal worship.
The macrocosm, identified with the Śrī-cakra and the individual.
The microcosm, identified with the universe.
A key factor in Samaya philosophy, along with bindu and kalā.
The transcendental point of potentiality; Śiva's power.
A factor in creation and identity contemplation.
The psychic energy centers in the subtle body.
The dormant spiritual energy at the base of the spine.
The three psychic knots that obstruct the flow of energy in the Suṣumnā.
The highest form of worship, the dissolution of the mind.
A practical application of antaryāga.
A Vedic precedent for antaryāga.
Refers to the traditional scriptures and schools of thought, particularly in Śaiva and Śākta traditions.
The tradition associated with the Kerala region.
The tradition associated with the Kaśmira region.
The tradition associated with the Gauḍa region.
Used in a quote from Tārā-khaṇḍa referring to the traditions of Kerala, Kaśmīra, and Gauḍa.
One of the three main philosophical divisions, often associated with external rituals and the worship of Kula (the ultimate reality manifested as Śakti).
One of the three main philosophical divisions, associated with internal, meditative worship (samayācāra).
The 'mixed' tradition that combines elements of both Kaula and Samaya.
The doctrinal basis of the Miśra and Samaya traditions.
From a verse listing the literature of the Kaula division.
A superior Kaula sect that uses rituals symbolically.
A Kaula sect given to 'crude' forms of worship.
A Kaula sect that identifies with Śiva/Śakti during worship.
A Kaula sect that worships in the nude.

complete_terminology_index.translation: A type of ascetic, possibly Buddhist or Jain
complete_terminology_index.context: A Kaula sect whose identity is uncertain.
Tantric practices that utilize forbidden or unconventional substances and rituals, such as the five 'ma-kāras'.
The five articles used in Vāmācāra rituals: 'matsya' (fish), 'māṁsa' (flesh), 'madya' (liquor), 'mudrā' (postures/cereals), and 'maithuna' (copulation).
The formal initiation by a master (guru) into a spiritual tradition, considered all-important.
The goal of realization according to the Paraśurāma-kalpa-sūtra.
Used to describe the three major territorial divisions of tantric literature (Viṣṇu-krānta, etc.).
The term for chapters in the Mahā-nirvāṇa-tantra.
A practice prescribed in the Subhagodaya.
